{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Robert F. Riley''' (December 22, 1935&ndash;March 4, 2000<ref>{{cite journal | title=Deaths&ndash;Robert Freed Riley | journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society | volume=47 | issue=6 | pages=679 | year=2000 | url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200006/people.pdf}}</ref>) was an American mathematician. He is known for his work in [[low-dimensional topology]] using computational tools and [[hyperbolic geometry]], being one of the inspirations for [[William Thurston]]'s later breakthroughs in [[3-dimensional topology]].{{sfn|Thurston|1982|p=360}} 

==Career==
Riley earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics from [[MIT]] in 1957; shortly thereafter he dropped out of the graduate program and went on to work in industry, eventually moving to Amsterdam in 1966. In 1968 he took a temporary position at the [[University of Southampton]].{{sfn|Brin|Jones|Singerman|2013}} He defended his Ph.D. at this institution in 1980, under the nominal direction of David Singerman.<ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=120399|title=Robert Riley}}</ref> For the next two years he occupied a postdoctoral position in [[Boulder, Colorado|Boulder]] where William Thurston was employed at the time, before moving on to Binghamton University as a professor.{{sfn|Brin|Jones|Singerman|2013}}

==Mathematical work==
Riley's research was in [[geometric topology]], especially in [[knot theory]], where he mostly studied [[Representation theory|representations]] of [[knot group]]s. Early on, following work of [[Ralph Fox]], he was interested in morphisms to finite groups. Later on in Southampton, considering <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb C)</math>-representations sending peripheral elements to parabolics led him to discover the [[hyperbolic 3-manifold|hyperbolic structure]] on the complement of the [[figure-eight knot]] and some others.{{sfn|Riley|1975a}}{{sfn|Riley|1975b}} This was one of the few examples of hyperbolic 3-manifolds that were available at the time, and as such it was one of the motivations which led to William Thurston's [[geometrisation conjecture]], which includes as a particular case a criterion for a knot complement to support a hyperbolic structure.{{sfn|Thurston|1982}} One notable feature of Riley's work is that it relied much on the assistance of a computer.{{sfn|Riley|2013}}
